key_facts: On November 1, 2024 at approximately 12:55 a.m., CHP Officers Santiago Meza-Gonzalez (#023295) and Jose Melano (#023054) found Plaintiff asleep in a stationary 2023 gray Tesla Model Y (rental, CA Plate 9EAX768, registered to PV Holding Corp.) parked on the unpaved dirt shoulder of eastbound I-580, approximately 0.3 miles west of Isabel Avenue, Livermore (CHP Case No. RJ68845, CAD No. 241101GG0064). Engine off, keys not in ignition, vehicle legally parked on freeway shoulder. **Plaintiff is pre-diabetic**, a condition that can physiologically produce signs mimicking alcohol intoxication: red/watery eyes, balance impairment, and altered time perception. Fourteen seconds after dashcam audio activated (00:56:09), before any welfare contact, Officer Melano speculatively declared 'I think it's booze' — no articulable basis documented. At 00:56:43 Melano opened the passenger door without warrant, consent, or lawful authority. The 62-minute dashcam recording (00:54:36–01:57:10) captures all material facts: Melano explicitly identifies the only liquid found as urine: 'Is it water? No this is piss. This is pee... I'm telling you it's piss. It smells like piss' (00:58:49–00:59:07); Officer Meza-Gonzalez refuses to smell the cup and never verbalizes alcohol odor throughout the entire encounter; no officer contemporaneously mentions alcohol odor from Plaintiff's breath or person in 62 minutes of recording. Plaintiff was handcuffed at 01:11:16; parole status disclosed by CHP Dispatch at 01:11:42 — after handcuffing, establishing post-hoc justification rather than articulable predicate. Arrest recorded at 01:12 a.m. under CVC §23152(a), citing CVC §40300.5 (warrantless arrest authority) despite zero observed volitional movement. Blood-draw warrant WAR913372 approved by Judge A. Sekany at 02:34 a.m.; two vials drawn by phlebotomist Aziza Ghaleb at 02:38 a.m. — a contradiction that directly undermines the subsequent 'Chemical Test Refusal' designation on the DS-367. Plaintiff booked at Santa Rita Jail under booking no. CAR913358 at 03:25 a.m. On November 5, 2024 — four days after arrest — Dublin CHP issued a formal Detention Certificate (Dublin CHP-01991, CHP Case No. RJ68845, CHP File No. 202400898) formally reclassifying the event as 'a detention only, not an arrest' under PC §849(b)(1) for 'insufficient grounds for making a criminal complaint.' **This Detention Certificate is legally equivalent to a judicial finding that no crime was committed.** The Alameda County DA declined to file any charges, confirming insufficient probable cause. By operation of PC §§849(c) and 849.5, the event ceased to be an 'arrest' as a matter of law. The APS suspension framework (CVC §§13353, 13353.2) conditions jurisdiction on a 'lawful arrest' as a non-waivable predicate — **a predicate irrevocably destroyed by operation of law more than two months before the January 24, 2025 APS hearing.** The DS-367 Chemical Test Refusal designation directly contradicts the existence of the blood draw warrant and blood sample collection, creating an internal logical impossibility. By January 24, 2025, the DMV's dual-prosecutor/adjudicator role had been judicially condemned in three separate appellate decisions: California DUI Lawyers Ass'n v. DMV, 77 Cal.App.5th 517 (Apr. 15, 2022) [33+ months before hearing]; Knudsen v. DMV, 101 Cal.App.5th 186 (Apr. 4, 2024) [9 months before hearing]; Clarke v. Gordon (Cal. Ct. App., Sept. 12, 2024, No. G062856) 2024 WL 4163081 [4 months before hearing, naming Defendant Gordon personally as respondent]. On February 11, 2025, Hearing Officer Diana Candelaria issued a four-page Notification of Findings and Decision (APS Case 34739340) that: **(1) fails to mention the Detention Certificate anywhere, despite it being the single most legally dispositive piece of evidence in the administrative record; (2) dismisses all of Plaintiff's constitutional and statutory arguments as 'unpersuasive' without reasoned analysis or citation to law; (3) mischaracterizes the factual record by stating 'No evidence was presented to the contrary.'** The decision imposes a one-year Class A CDL suspension (Feb. 20, 2025 – Feb. 19, 2026), $125 reissue fee (CVC §§14904, 14906), and three-year SR-22 requirement (CVC §16430). Plaintiff had been employed by Centerline Drivers, LLC (Lily Transportation–Toyota Dedicated route, San Ramon, CA) beginning October 30, 2024 — exactly two days before the incident — at $33.35/hour regular time and $50.03/hour premium time (approximately $72,000/year earning capacity). The Class A CDL suspension with commercial disqualification terminated this employment and caused cascading economic harm. Total documented damages exceed $326,000, accruing daily.

risk: Moot as to this (dismissed) docket — the analysis below was never tested past the magistrate's adverse F&R and now carries forward into Matter 33's fresh complaint instead. Historical record: **Favorable, rebutted qualified immunity on multiple independent grounds.** Absolute immunity unavailable: Candelaria's conduct was prosecutorial and advocacy in nature, not judicial. Absolute immunity protects only judicial functions performed with structural independence (Forrester v. White, 484 U.S. 219 (1988); Cleavinger v. Saxner, 474 U.S. 193 (1985); In re Groat, 425 F.3d 256 (4th Cir. 2005)). Here, Candelaria: (1) advocated for the DMV/officers by ignoring exculpatory Detention Certificate; (2) operated under structural conflict of interest (DMV's prosecutorial interest in defending officers vs. adjudicatory duty); (3) issued conclusory decision defending officers' narrative rather than neutrally evaluating record. **Qualified immunity also unavailable**: Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982) requires predicate clearly established at time of violation. The following constitutional rights were unambiguously established well before January 24, 2025: (1) **CDL as protected property interest in liberty** (Bell v. Burson, 402 U.S. 535 (1971) — 55 years before violation; Mackey v. Montrym, 443 U.S. 1 (1979) — 46 years before violation); (2) **fair hearing before neutral decisionmaker** (Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) — 49 years before violation; Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35 (1975) — 50 years before violation; Tumey v. Ohio, 273 U.S. 510 (1927) — 98 years before violation); (3) **warrantless DUI arrest under CVC §40300.5 requires observed volitional movement** (Mercer v. DMV, 53 Cal.3d 753 (1991) — 34 years before violation; binding California Supreme Court precedent directly addressing §40300.5); (4) **PC §849(b)(1) release reclassifies arrest as 'detention only' by mandatory statutory language** — no discretion or ambiguity (PC §849(b)(1), §849(c), §849.5); (5) **refusal suspension under CVC §13353 requires 'lawful arrest' as jurisdictional predicate** (Music v. Department of Motor Vehicles, 221 Cal.App.3d 841, 850 (1990) — 36 years before violation); (6) **dual-role APS framework violates structural due process** (California DUI Lawyers Ass'n v. DMV, 77 Cal.App.5th 517 (Apr. 15, 2022) — 33+ months before hearing; Knudsen v. DMV, 101 Cal.App.5th 186 (Apr. 4, 2024) — 9 months before hearing; Clarke v. Gordon, 2024 WL 4163081 (Sept. 12, 2024) — 4 months before hearing, naming Defendant Gordon personally as respondent). **Structural error doctrine** (Knudsen): Under the Ninth Circuit structural error framework, no showing of actual prejudice is required — the structural bias itself is the constitutional violation. Candelaria's simultaneous role as DMV's prosecutorial advocate and adjudicator is structural error per se. **The Detention Certificate is the strongest possible evidence and the single most legally dispositive piece**: CHP's own agency, not an outside critic, formally repudiated the arrest via mandatory statutory certificate. Candelaria's four-page decision fails to mention it even once — **not an oversight, but evidence of predetermined outcome and denial of meaningful hearing.** Mischaracterization of record ('No evidence was presented to the contrary') is demonstrably false — evidence populated the entire administrative file and was presented at the January 24, 2025 hearing. This misstatement satisfies recklessness standard and supports punitive damages against Candelaria individually. **Cross-claim leverage**: if FAC survives motion to dismiss, the structural bias findings and clearly established law precedents create significant pressure on Defendant Gordon (DMV Director) to settle rather than defend a system he statutorily oversees and for which he has receipt of notice via Clarke v. Gordon naming him personally.
